Hormones 
Experiments by pioneering scientists have greatly improved our 
understanding of the body’s chemical messengers 
 
Hormones are remarkable chemicals, 
secreted into our blood by organs 
called endocrine glands. They control 
almost everything our body does, 
from our growth and development to 
our impulses and mood, from how 
often we sleep to how quickly our 
heart beats. There are even hormones 
that regulate our hormones.  
Yet until the start of the 20th 
century, most scientists had no idea 
these chemicals even existed, let 
alone how they worked. The story of 
endocrinology – the study of 
hormones – begins in 1849 with a 
German scientist called Arnold 
Berthold. In what is now recognised 
as the first endocrinal experiment, 
Berthold discovered that there must 
be a substance carried in the 
bloodstream of cockerels that 
triggered their aggressive male 
behaviour and the growth of their 
characteristic red plumage.  
Despite the significance of 
Berthold’s findings, his results went 
largely unnoticed for nearly half a 
century. Then, in 1891, George 
Redmayne Murray announced that 
he had managed to cure the medical 
condition known as myxedema. Now 
recognised as underactivity of the 
thyroid gland, the condition causes 
alarming swelling of the hands and 
eyes. Murray’s treatment involved 
taking a sheep, obtaining extracts 
from its thyroid gland, and then 
injecting this into patients. This was 
the first effective application of 
endocrinology in conventional 
medicine. By 1895, George Oliver and 
Edward Schafer had shown that 
injections of extracts of the adrenal 
glands and pituitary glands raised 
animals’ blood pressure. This was 
further proof that secretions released 
by glands could create important 
effects elsewhere in the body.  
Despite mounting evidence of an 
internal chemical control system, the 
British Medical Association was still 
reluctant to accept the idea. The 
prevailing wisdom since ancient times 
was that the nervous system 
controlled the body’s functions, and it 
was difficult for people to accept that 
this might not be the case. 
Thankfully, in 1902, a defining 
experiment conducted by physiologist 
Ernest Starling and his brother-in-
law William Bayliss proved beyond 
doubt that chemicals in the blood 
could affect the behaviour of organs 
independently of the nervous system. 
While carrying out research into the 
digestive systems of animals, they 
discovered that an organ called the 
duodenum, close to the stomach, was 
releasing a chemical substance that 
was entering the bloodstream and 
acting on other organs. They called 
this substance ‘secretin’. Three years 
later, in a lecture to the Royal College 
of Physicians, Starling referred to

3 
 
such chemicals as ‘hormones’, based 
on the ancient Greek word for ‘I 
excite’, and the term stuck.  
From here, advancement in 
endocrinology began to gather pace. 
In 1921, Frederick Banting and 
Charles Best identified insulin, the 
hormone which tells the body to 
absorb sugar from the bloodstream. 
Their findings would lead to a 
treatment that still saves millions of 
lives today. Before Banting and Best’s 
discovery, people suffering from 
diabetes – the inability to produce 
enough insulin – often succumbed to 
a slow and painful death at a young 
age. In their groundbreaking 
experiment, the pair caused a dog to 
become diabetic by the removal of the 
organ known as the pancreas. 
Convinced that this organ had a key 
function in the production of 
hormones, the pair then injected the 
animal with secretions from certain 
cells of another dog’s pancreas. The 
animal’s blood sugar levels quickly 
returned to normal. Within a year of 
this discovery, they were 
administering the hormone insulin to 
human patients, and within two 
years, a pharmaceutical company 
was making enough to treat all the 
diabetics in North America.  
Modern endocrinology was now in 
full swing, and there were numerous 
breakthroughs throughout the rest of 
the 20th century. Many of them came 
thanks to the ability to measure tiny 
quantities of hormones circulating in 
the blood. Such precise 
measurements would be impossible 
without a technique called 
‘radioimmunoassay’, developed by US 
physicist and Nobel prize-winner 
Rosalyn Yalow. Her technique, which 
uses specially designed antibodies to 
bind to biological molecules of 
interest, allowed fellow prize-winners 
Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally 
to measure minute concentrations of 
pituitary hormones in the blood. This 
work was vital in understanding the 
pituitary gland’s role as a regulator of 
other hormone glands. The pituitary 
links the brain with the rest of the 
endocrine system, and is a crucial 
connection between our senses and 
the body’s chemical response system.  
In recent years, our 
understanding of hormones has 
grown immensely. Work is ongoing to 
unravel the complex relationships 
between hormones and the great 
challenges of our era like obesity, 
cardiovascular disease, depression 
and aging. To date, around 80 of 
these remarkable chemicals have 
been identified.
